claim: The mTORC1 signaling pathway balances the expression of two Trim9/TRIM9 isoforms through APA regulation in human and mouse.
source: Here we report the discovery that the mTORC1 signaling pathway balances the expression of two Trim9/TRIM9 isoforms through APA regulation in human and mouse.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: CFIm components, CPSF6 and NUDT21, promote the short Trim9/TRIM9 isoform (Trim9-S/TRIM9-S) expression.
source: We showed that CFIm components, CPSF6 and NUDT21, promote the short Trim9/TRIM9 isoform (Trim9-S/TRIM9-S) expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An evolutionarily conserved twin UGUA motif, UGUAYUGUA, exists in TRIM9-S polyadenylation site (PAS).
source: In addition, we identified an evolutionarily conserved twin UGUA motif, UGUAYUGUA, in TRIM9-S polyadenylation site (PAS) that is critical for its regulation by CPSF6.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence analysis and conservation data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The twin UGUA motif in TRIM9-S PAS is critical for its regulation by CPSF6.
source: In addition, we identified an evolutionarily conserved twin UGUA motif, UGUAYUGUA, in TRIM9-S polyadenylation site (PAS) that is critical for its regulation by CPSF6.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: CPSF6-regulated PASs with similar twin UGUA motifs exist in human genes including BMPR1B, MOB4, and BRD4-L.
source: We found additional CPSF6-regulated PASs with similar twin UGUA motifs in human and experimentally validated the twin UGUA motif functionality in BMPR1B, MOB4, and BRD4-L.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by PAPERCLIP profiling and reporter assays shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Inserting a twin UGUA motif into a heterologous PAS is sufficient to confer regulation by CPSF6 and mTORC1.
source: Importantly, we showed that inserting a twin UGUA motif into a heterologous PAS was sufficient to confer regulation by CPSF6 and mTORC1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by reporter assays using JUNB PAS shown in Figure 7.

claim: Co-expression of Cdc42 exon 6 and exon 7 isoforms is crucial for normal neuron morphogenesis.
source: For example, in neurons, co-expression of Cdc42 exon 6 and exon 7 isoforms (both are alternative 3′ terminal exons) is crucial for normal morphogenesis as loss of either isoform results in abnormal development of axons and dendrites (Yap et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Yap et al., 2016).

claim: Loss of either Cdc42 exon 6 or exon 7 isoform results in abnormal development of axons and dendrites.
source: For example, in neurons, co-expression of Cdc42 exon 6 and exon 7 isoforms (both are alternative 3′ terminal exons) is crucial for normal morphogenesis as loss of either isoform results in abnormal development of axons and dendrites (Yap et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Yap et al., 2016).

claim: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) is an important mechanism to generate RNA isoforms with different 3′ ends.
source: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) is an important mechanism to generate RNA isoforms with different 3′ ends (Gruber and Zavolan, 2019; Mitschka and Mayr, 2022; Tian and Manley, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: CFIm is not essential for the cleavage reaction but has an outsized role in regulating APA as a sequence-dependent activator of mRNA 3′-end processing.
source: The mRNA 3′-end processing factor CFIm is not essential for the cleavage reaction but has an outsized role in regulating APA as a sequence-dependent activator of mRNA 3′-end processing (Boreikaite et al., 2022; Schmidt et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: The human CFIm consists of a small subunit, CFIm25 (encoded by the NUDT21 gene), which directly binds to the UGUA motif.
source: The human CFIm consists of two subunits: a small subunit, CFIm25 (encoded by the NUDT21 gene), which directly binds to the UGUA motif, and two alternative large subunits, CFIm68 (encoded by the CPSF6 gene) and CFIm59 (encoded by the CPSF7 gene), which activate 3′-end processing by interacting with CPSF, one of the essential mRNA 3′-end processing factors (Yang et al., 2011a; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published studies (Yang et al., 2011a; Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: CFIm68 (encoded by the CPSF6 gene) and CFIm59 (encoded by the CPSF7 gene) are two alternative large subunits of human CFIm that activate 3′-end processing by interacting with CPSF.
source: The human CFIm consists of two subunits: a small subunit, CFIm25 (encoded by the NUDT21 gene), which directly binds to the UGUA motif, and two alternative large subunits, CFIm68 (encoded by the CPSF6 gene) and CFIm59 (encoded by the CPSF7 gene), which activate 3′-end processing by interacting with CPSF, one of the essential mRNA 3′-end processing factors (Yang et al., 2011a; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published studies (Yang et al., 2011a; Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: Loss of NUDT21 or CPSF6, but not CPSF7, resulted in widespread and overlapping APA alterations in cells.
source: It has been shown that loss of NUDT21 or CPSF6, but not CPSF7, resulted in widespread and overlapping APA alterations in cells (Ghosh et al., 2022; Gruber et al., 2012; Hwang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: CFIm59 is a weaker activator of 3′-end processing compared with CFIm68.
source: This is consistent with the finding that CFIm59 is a weaker activator of 3′-end processing compared with CFIm68 (Zhu et al., 2018) and highlights the important roles of NUDT21 and CPSF6 in APA regulation.
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: APA changes from loss of NUDT21 or CPSF6 are predominantly proximal shifts that lead to 3′ UTR shortening or expression of truncated proteins.
source: Notably, APA changes from loss of NUDT21 or CPSF6 are predominantly proximal shifts that lead to 3′ UTR shortening or expression of truncated proteins (Gruber et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014), which can be explained by the skewed distribution of the UGUA motif that favors the distal PAS in CFIm target mRNAs (Ghosh et al., 2022; Hwang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: The skewed distribution of the UGUA motif favors the distal PAS in CFIm target mRNAs.
source: Notably, APA changes from loss of NUDT21 or CPSF6 are predominantly proximal shifts that lead to 3′ UTR shortening or expression of truncated proteins (Gruber et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014), which can be explained by the skewed distribution of the UGUA motif that favors the distal PAS in CFIm target mRNAs (Ghosh et al., 2022; Hwang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: The mTORC1 signaling pathway plays a central role in regulating cell metabolism.
source: The mTORC1 signaling pathway plays a central role in regulating cell metabolism and hyperactive mTORC1 causes a group of neurodevelopmental disorders termed 'mTORopathies' with shared clinical manifestations (Crino, 2016; Lipton and Sahin, 2014; Liu and Sabatini, 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Hyperactive mTORC1 causes a group of neurodevelopmental disorders termed 'mTORopathies' with shared clinical manifestations.
source: The mTORC1 signaling pathway plays a central role in regulating cell metabolism and hyperactive mTORC1 causes a group of neurodevelopmental disorders termed 'mTORopathies' with shared clinical manifestations (Crino, 2016; Lipton and Sahin, 2014; Liu and Sabatini, 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2.
source: One of the best-studied mTORopathies is Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC), which is caused by loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2, both of which are mTORC1 inhibitors (Salussolia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Salussolia et al., 2019).

claim: TSC1 and TSC2 are mTORC1 inhibitors.
source: One of the best-studied mTORopathies is Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC), which is caused by loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2, both of which are mTORC1 inhibitors (Salussolia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Salussolia et al., 2019).

claim: Hundreds of mRNAs with shortened 3′ UTRs were identified in Tsc1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, a recent RNA-seq study identified hundreds of mRNAs with shortened 3′ UTRs in Tsc1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Chang et al., 2015), which is reminiscent of the aforementioned APA changes from loss of NUDT21 or CPSF6.
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Chang et al., 2015).

claim: In starvation, repression of the mTORC1 signaling allows two downstream kinases, CDK8 and CLK2, to phosphorylate CPSF6 in Drosophila.
source: Subsequently, a direct link between the mTORC1 pathway and CPSF6 was discovered in Drosophila—in starvation, repression of the mTORC1 signaling allows two downstream kinases, CDK8 and CLK2, to phosphorylate CPSF6, which is required for its nuclear localization to promote 3′ UTR lengthening of autophagy genes Atg1 and Atg8a (Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Tang et al., 2018).

claim: CPSF6 phosphorylation by CDK8 and CLK2 is required for its nuclear localization to promote 3′ UTR lengthening of autophagy genes Atg1 and Atg8a in Drosophila.
source: Subsequently, a direct link between the mTORC1 pathway and CPSF6 was discovered in Drosophila—in starvation, repression of the mTORC1 signaling allows two downstream kinases, CDK8 and CLK2, to phosphorylate CPSF6, which is required for its nuclear localization to promote 3′ UTR lengthening of autophagy genes Atg1 and Atg8a (Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Tang et al., 2018).

claim: The regulation of CPSF6 by CDK8 and CLK2 is present in human MCF7 cells and is required for starvation-induced autophagy.
source: The regulation of CPSF6 by CDK8 and CLK2 was also present in human MCF7 cells and was required for starvation-induced autophagy (Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Tang et al., 2018).

claim: Primary morbidity for TSC patients comes from central nervous system involvement.
source: Because primary morbidity for TSC patients comes from central nervous system involvement (Salussolia et al., 2019), we sought to investigate how hyperactive mTORC1 impacts the APA landscape in different brain cell types in vivo using cTag-PAPERCLIP and the widely used Tsc1 conditional knockout mice (Bateup et al., 2013; Ercan et al., 2017; Kwiatkowski et al., 2002; Meikle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Salussolia et al., 2019).

claim: Trim9/TRIM9 encodes a neuronally enriched E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates neuron morphogenesis.
source: Trim9/TRIM9 encodes a neuronally enriched E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates neuron morphogenesis (Winkle et al., 2014; Winkle et al., 2016), but it was not previously reported to be regulated by mTORC1 or CFIm.
evidence: This is cited from published studies (Winkle et al., 2014; Winkle et al., 2016).

claim: Trim9/TRIM9 was not previously reported to be regulated by mTORC1 or CFIm.
source: Trim9/TRIM9 encodes a neuronally enriched E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates neuron morphogenesis (Winkle et al., 2014; Winkle et al., 2016), but it was not previously reported to be regulated by mTORC1 or CFIm.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the manuscript.

claim: Systemic AAV injection of pAAV-Camk2a-iCre turns on PABP-GFP expression in excitatory neurons for cTag-PAPERCLIP profiling in both Tsc1-WT and Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice.
source: We expected pAAV-Camk2a-iCre injection to (1) turn on PABP-GFP expression in excitatory neurons for cTag-PAPERCLIP profiling in both Tsc1-WT and Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice and (2) knock Tsc1 out and activate the mTORC1 signaling in excitatory neurons in Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice.
evidence: This is stated as an expected outcome and verified by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Systemic AAV injection of pAAV-Camk2a-iCre knocks Tsc1 out and activates the mTORC1 signaling in excitatory neurons in Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice.
source: We expected pAAV-Camk2a-iCre injection to (1) turn on PABP-GFP expression in excitatory neurons for cTag-PAPERCLIP profiling in both Tsc1-WT and Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice and (2) knock Tsc1 out and activate the mTORC1 signaling in excitatory neurons in Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice.
evidence: This is stated as an expected outcome and verified by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tsc1 mRNA expression was strongly reduced (>80%, 44.9 cpm to 8.6 cpm, p<0.01) in the injected Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice.
source: As expected, Tsc1 mRNA expression was strongly reduced (>80%, 44.9 cpm to 8.6 cpm, p<0.01) in the injected Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice (designated as Tsc1-KO hereafter) while both Tsc2 and Mtor mRNAs were expressed at similar levels in the injected mice of both genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by cTag-PAPERCLIP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tsc2 and Mtor mRNAs were expressed at similar levels in the injected mice of both genotypes.
source: As expected, Tsc1 mRNA expression was strongly reduced (>80%, 44.9 cpm to 8.6 cpm, p<0.01) in the injected Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mice (designated as Tsc1-KO hereafter) while both Tsc2 and Mtor mRNAs were expressed at similar levels in the injected mice of both genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by cTag-PAPERCLIP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PS6 in the brain cortex was strongly increased in an injected Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mouse when compared to an uninjected mouse of the same genotype.
source: As expected, PS6 in the brain cortex was strongly increased in an injected Tsc1-floxed cTag-PABP mouse when compared to an uninjected mouse of the same genotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The magnitude of the PS6 increase is identical between AAV injection and genetic breeding.
source: We found that the magnitude of the PS6 increase is identical between AAV injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and genetic breeding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that Cre delivery efficiency from systemic AAV injection is equivalent to that of genetic breeding.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Cre delivery efficiency from systemic AAV injection is equivalent to that of genetic breeding.
source: We found that the magnitude of the PS6 increase is identical between AAV injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and genetic breeding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that Cre delivery efficiency from systemic AAV injection is equivalent to that of genetic breeding.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PS6 levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Systemic AAV injection is an effective way to deliver cell type-specific Cre recombinases for cTag-PAPERCLIP profiling.
source: Therefore, we concluded that systemic AAV injection is an effective way to deliver cell type-specific Cre recombinases for cTag-PAPERCLIP profiling.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 135 genes with two PASs significantly changed their APA preference (FDR < 0.05, >2-fold change) in Tsc1-KO cortical excitatory neurons.
source: From the cTag-PAPERCLIP experiments (two biological replicates for each genotype), we identified 135 genes with two PASs that significantly changed their APA preference (FDR < 0.05, >2-fold change) in Tsc1-KO cortical excitatory neurons—30 shifted proximally while 105 shifted distally (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by cTag-PAPERCLIP data analysis.

claim: 30 genes shifted proximally while 105 shifted distally in Tsc1-KO cortical excitatory neurons.
source: From the cTag-PAPERCLIP experiments (two biological replicates for each genotype), we identified 135 genes with two PASs that significantly changed their APA preference (FDR < 0.05, >2-fold change) in Tsc1-KO cortical excitatory neurons—30 shifted proximally while 105 shifted distally (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by cTag-PAPERCLIP data analysis.

claim: Trim9 is the only gene that satisfied both criteria of switching the major PAS and being CDS-APA.
source: Only one gene from the list, Trim9, fulfilled both criteria.
evidence: This is stated based on the filtering strategy applied to the cTag-PAPERCLIP data.

claim: Tsc1 knockout in mouse cortical excitatory neurons causes a shift toward Trim9-L mRNA expression.
source: Tsc1 knockout in mouse cortical excitatory neurons causes a shift toward Trim9-L mRNA expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by cTag-PAPERCLIP data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Trim9-L is the full-length isoform while Trim9-S uses an upstream PAS to skip exons 8–14 and lacks the SPRY domain at the protein level.
source: Trim9-L is the full-length isoform while Trim9-S uses an upstream PAS to skip exons 8–14 and lacks the SPRY domain at the protein level (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the GENCODE annotations and protein domain analysis shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The SPRY domain is commonly found in TRIM family proteins and is implicated in protein–protein interaction.
source: The SPRY domain is commonly found in TRIM family proteins and is implicated in protein–protein interaction (Ozato et al., 2008; Perfetto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published studies (Ozato et al., 2008; Perfetto et al., 2013).

claim: A shift toward Trim9-L protein expression was observed in the Tsc1-KO cTag-PABP mouse.
source: In parallel with the cTag-PAPERCLIP results, a shift toward Trim9-L protein expression was also observed in the Tsc1-KO cTag-PABP mouse (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A similar shift toward Trim9-L mRNA expression was observed in the Camk2a-Cre; Tsc1fl/fl mouse compared to Tsc1fl/fl mouse.
source: Although this assay is not cell-type-specific like cTag-PAPERCLIP, a similar shift toward Trim9-L mRNA expression was also observed (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TRIM9-L mRNA expression was increased by more than 1.6-fold in TSC2-KO NSCs compared to WT NSCs.
source: We found that TRIM9-L mRNA expression was increased by more than 1.6-fold in TSC2-KO NSCs compared to WT NSCs (Figure 1F, left panel, 17.2 cpm to 28.4 cpm, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The TRIM9-L/TRIM9-S ratio was consistently higher in TSC2-KO NSCs compared to WT NSCs in all replicates.
source: Moreover, the TRM9-L/TRIM9-S ratio was consistently higher in TSC2-KO NSCs compared to WT NSCs in all replicates (Figure 1F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In both mouse and human neurons, hyperactive mTORC1 causes an APA shift in Trim9/TRIM9 that favors full-length Trim9-L/TRIM9-L expression.
source: Taken together, these results show that, in both mouse and human neurons, hyperactive mTORC1 causes an APA shift in Trim9/TRIM9 that favors full-length Trim9-L/TRIM9-L expression.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Torin 1 treatment successfully shut down mTORC1 and eliminated PS6 in N2a cells.
source: As expected, Torin 1 treatment successfully shut down mTORC1 and eliminated PS6 in N2a cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Torin 1-treated N2a cells, Trim9 expression was consistently shifted toward Trim9-S with similar magnitudes at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: As predicted from our in vivo findings (low mTORC1 activities would favor Trim9-S expression), in Torin 1-treated N2a cells, Trim9 expression was consistently shifted toward Trim9-S with similar magnitudes at both mRNA (Figure 2B, right panel) and protein (Figure 2C and D) levels.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: Either siTsc1 or siTsc2 transfection could increase mTORC1 activities in N2a cells.
source: As evidenced by a rise in PS6 (Figure 2E), we found that either siTsc1 or siTsc2 transfection could increase mTORC1 activities in N2a cells, which then favored Trim9-L mRNA expression as expected (Figure 2F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increased mTORC1 activities from siTsc1 or siTsc2 transfection favored Trim9-L mRNA expression in N2a cells.
source: As evidenced by a rise in PS6 (Figure 2E), we found that either siTsc1 or siTsc2 transfection could increase mTORC1 activities in N2a cells, which then favored Trim9-L mRNA expression as expected (Figure 2F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Low mTORC1 activities promoted TRIM9-S expression while high mTORC1 activities favored TRIM9-L expression in BE2C cells.
source: As seen in mouse cortical neurons in vivo and in N2a cells, low mTORC1 activities indeed promoted TRIM9-S expression while high mTORC1 activities favored TRIM9-L expression in BE2C cells (Figure 2G, right panel, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The mTORC1 signaling pathway controls the balance between the two Trim9/TRIM9 isoforms in both mouse and human.
source: Taken together, our cell culture studies recapitulated the Trim9 APA shift from Tsc1-KO mice and showed that the mTORC1 signaling pathway controls the balance between the two Trim9/TRIM9 isoforms in both mouse and human.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Loss of Cpsf6 strongly decreased the abundance of Trim9-S mRNA but did not change Trim9-L mRNA expression in N2a cells.
source: Interestingly, loss of Cpsf6 had different effects on the two Trim9 isoforms: it strongly decreased the abundance of Trim9-S mRNA but did not change Trim9-L mRNA expression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nudt21 loss of function by siRNA transfection phenocopied loss of Cpsf6: Trim9-S mRNA expression was decreased but Trim9-L mRNA expression did not statistically significantly change in N2a cells.
source: Next, we induce Nudt21 loss of function in N2a cells by siRNA transfection (Figure 3C), which phenocopied loss of Cpsf6: Trim9-S mRNA expression was decreased but Trim9-L mRNA expression did not statistically significantly change (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both CPSF6 and NUDT21 knockdown lowered TRIM9-S expression in BE2C cells.
source: Both treatments similarly lowered TRIM9-S expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CPSF6 knockdown significantly increased TRIM9-L expression in BE2C cells.
source: However, unlike in N2a cells, CPSF6 knockdown also significantly increased TRIM9-L expression in BE2C cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both CPSF6 and NUDT21 promote Trim9-S/TRIM9-S expression in mouse and human cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that both CPSF6 and NUDT21 promote Trim9-S/TRIM9-S expression in mouse and human cells.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In control N2a cells, Torin 1 treatment shifted Trim9 expression toward Trim9-S.
source: In control N2a cells, Torin 1 treatment shifted Trim9 expression toward Trim9-S as expected (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The shift toward Trim9-S from Torin 1 treatment was lost in Cpsf6 loss-of-function N2a cells.
source: However, the shift was lost in Cpsf6 loss-of-function N2a cells (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a requirement of Cpsf6.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In control siRNA-transfected N2a cells, Torin 1 treatment shifted Trim9 expression toward Trim9-S.
source: In control siRNA-transfected N2a cells, Torin 1 treatment again shifted Trim9 expression toward Trim9-S (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In Nudt21 siRNA-transfected N2a cells, Torin 1 treatment did not favor Trim9-S expression but significantly shifted the balance toward Trim9-L instead.
source: In contrast, in Nudt21 siRNA-transfected N2a cells, Torin 1 treatment did not favor Trim9-S expression but significantly shifted the balance toward Trim9-L instead (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Cpsf6 and Nudt21 are both required for the observed regulation of Trim9 isoforms by the mTORC1 signaling pathway.
source: Altogether, these results support that Cpsf6 and Nudt21 are both required for the observed regulation of Trim9 isoforms by the mTORC1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both mouse Trim9-S PAS and human TRIM9-S PAS contain a 5′ twin UGUA motif (UGUAYUGUA; Y=C in human and T in mouse) followed by two downstream UGUA motifs, for a total of four UGUA motifs.
source: Both mouse Trim9-S PAS and human TRIM9-S PAS contain a 5′ twin UGUA motif (UGUAYUGUA; Y=C in human and T in mouse) followed by two downstream UGUA motifs, for a total of four UGUA motifs (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three of the four UGUA motifs in Trim9-S/TRIM9-S PAS, including the twin UGUA motif, were conserved between mouse and human.
source: Interestingly, three of the four UGUA motifs, including the twin UGUA motif, were conserved between mouse and human.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of CPSF6 approximately halved TRIM9-S PAS usage.
source: Next, we performed reporter assays using all three TRIM9-S PAS reporters with the following results: (1) loss of CPSF6 approximately halved TRIM9-S PAS usage (Figure 4F, 51% decrease).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mutations in the twin UGUA motif strongly decreased TRIM9-S PAS usage.
source: (2) Mutations in the twin UGUA motif strongly decreased TRIM9-S PAS usage (Figure 4G, group 1 vs. group 2, 73% decrease).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mutations in the other two UGUA motifs together had no effects on TRIM9-S PAS usage.
source: (3) Mutations in the other two UGUA motifs together had no effects on TRIM9-S PAS usage (Figure 4G, group 1 vs. group 3).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Loss of CPSF6 did not statistically significantly change the usage of TRIM9-S PAS with mutated twin UGUA motif.
source: (4) Loss of CPSF6 did not statistically significantly change the usage of TRIM9-S PAS with mutated twin UGUA motif (Figure 4G, group 2 vs. group 4, p=0.12).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CPSF6 promotes TRIM9-S PAS usage mostly through the twin UGUA motif.
source: Altogether, these results support that CPSF6 promotes TRIM9-S PAS usage mostly through the twin UGUA motif, which was evolutionarily conserved in multiple mammalian species including armadillo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is concluded based on the reporter assay data shown in Figure 4 and conservation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The twin UGUA motif in TRIM9-S PAS was evolutionarily conserved in multiple mammalian species including armadillo.
source: Altogether, these results support that CPSF6 promotes TRIM9-S PAS usage mostly through the twin UGUA motif, which was evolutionarily conserved in multiple mammalian species including armadillo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by conservation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutations in the first UGUA decreased TRIM9-S PAS usage but the effects were significantly weaker than those from mutations in both UGUAs.
source: Mutations in the first UGUA decreased TRIM9-S PAS usage but the effects were significantly weaker than those from mutations in both UGUAs (Figure 4I, MU1 vs. MU12, 34% vs. 75% decrease, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Mutations in the second UGUA consistently but very modestly increased TRIM9-S PAS usage.
source: In contrast, mutations in the second UGUA consistently but very modestly increased TRIM9-S PAS usage (Figure 4I, MU2: 7% increase).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The effects from individual UGUAs of the twin UGUA motif are not additive and neither of them is solely responsible for the full effects from the entire twin UGUA motif.
